title: The Third Will
premise: True-crime podcaster Ansel Brightwater built her reputation closing cold cases no one else would touch, but her latest investigation—the thirty-year-old disappearance of heiress Marguerite Voss—turns personal when a fresh corpse surfaces wearing clothes stolen from Ansel's own closet, each garment a piece of evidence from the original case. As she digs into the Voss family's tangled wills, she realizes the killer is someone who has studied the file as obsessively as she has: her own estranged half-sister, Wren, who survived the original crime as a child and has spent decades staging a revenge that frames Ansel for murders she didn't commit. In the climax at the derelict Voss estate, Ansel chooses exposure over survival, broadcasting the truth live to force Wren's surrender, and in the aftermath discovers the 'third will' names not an heir but a guardian—leaving Ansel, reluctantly and irrevocably, keeper of a found family she never expected.
about_author: Ines Sterling is the pen name of a former estate paralegal who spent a decade cataloguing disputed inheritances before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries about documents, secrets, and the families paperwork creates, from a farmhouse full of rescued animals.

chapters.title: The Coldest File
chapters.summary: Ansel Brightwater, POV. Ansel launches season five of her podcast with the 1994 Voss disappearance, promising listeners she never opens a case she can't close. Archival tapes reveal a child witness who was never named. Beat: confident showmanship undercut by a flicker of unease about why this file was sealed.

chapters.title: Clothes That Aren't Mine
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV. A body is found in the harbor town of Salt Hollow dressed in garments pulled from Ansel's own closet—each item matching evidence photos from 1994. Police treat her as suspect, then consultant. Beat: violation and vertigo; her invisibility, her armor, has been breached.

chapters.title: Detective Okafor
chapters.summary: Detective Ifeoma Okafor, POV. Okafor, who closed two of Ansel's podcast cases years ago, grudgingly shares the sealed file. The child witness's identity is redacted—but the redaction was added decades after the fact. Beat: wary alliance; two professionals circling the same lie.

chapters.title: The First Will
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV. At the Voss estate archive, Ansel studies patriarch Edmund Voss's will, which disinherited his daughter Marguerite weeks before she vanished. A caretaker mentions a 'second paper' Edmund burned. Beat: obsession kindling; the inheritance isn't money, it's silence.

chapters.title: Listener Number Nine
chapters.summary: Okafor, POV. Forensics link the harbor corpse to a retired archivist who once handled the Voss file. His download history shows he emailed the case documents to nine accounts—one belonging to 'W.' Beat: dread tightening; the killer is curating an audience.

chapters.title: Salt Hollow Secrets
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV. Ansel canvasses the town and finds a former housekeeper who lets slip that Marguerite had a child no one spoke of—a girl taken in quietly after the disappearance. Beat: grief surfacing through small-town complicity; everyone survived by forgetting.

chapters.title: The Second Body
chapters.summary: Okafor, POV. A second victim, dressed again in Ansel's clothes, is found posed inside the Voss mausoleum beside Marguerite's empty coffin. The staging mirrors page forty-one of the case file—a page only recently unsealed. Beat: horror sharpening into certainty that the killer reads along with them.

chapters.title: What I Kept
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV. Interrogated again, Ansel admits on record what she's hidden: she grew up in foster care near Salt Hollow and has no memory of ages four to six. Beat: vulnerability cracked open; her own past is a redacted document.

chapters.title: The Podcast Trap
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV. Ansel airs a deliberately false detail about the case, hoping the killer's corrections will expose their access. Within hours, an anonymous email corrects her—using phrasing from a private police memo. Beat: grim triumph curdling into fear; they're inside every room.

chapters.title: Okafor's Doubt
chapters.summary: Okafor, POV. Internal affairs questions Okafor's leaks; the memo could only have come from her desk. Suspended, she keeps working off-book with Ansel. Beat: loyalty tested; both women now stand outside the systems that defined them.

chapters.title: The Housekeeper's Box
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV. The dying housekeeper gives Ansel a shoebox: photographs of two little girls at the Voss estate, one clearly Marguerite's daughter, the other—Ansel. Beat: devastating recognition; she wasn't investigating the case, she was in it.

chapters.title: Sister, Stranger
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV. Records confirm it: Wren Voss, Marguerite's hidden daughter, and Ansel shared a foster placement for one year before Ansel was adopted out and Wren vanished back into the system. Beat: found family inverted—the sister she never knew has been watching her for years.

chapters.title: Contact
chapters.summary: Wren (unnamed, first person), POV. A chilling interlude: Wren explains, calmly, why Ansel was chosen—not as a target but as a witness who finally deserves to see. Beat: intimacy and menace braided together; the reader understands her before condemning her.

chapters.title: The Burned Paper
chapters.summary: Okafor, POV. Okafor traces the archivist's final research: Edmund Voss wrote a second will naming Marguerite's daughter sole heir—and a third document, never filed, appointing a guardian if the girl couldn't be found. Beat: revelation accelerating; the inheritance was always about custody, not cash.

chapters.title: Framed
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV. Police find Ansel's fingerprints on evidence from both murders. Arrest imminent, she goes underground with Okafor's help. Beat: desperation; the hunter is now the hunted, and the law itself is a weapon against her.

chapters.title: What Survival Cost
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Flashback chapters within Wren's account: the night Marguerite died, the uncle who killed her to void the second will, the foster home where Wren learned that surviving meant disappearing. Beat: tragic sympathy; the price of her survival was becoming no one.

chapters.title: The Uncle's Confession
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV. Following Wren's breadcrumbs, Ansel locates a taped deathbed confession from the uncle—an heir under the first will—admitting Marguerite's murder. But the tape also proves Wren witnessed everything at age seven. Beat: the case closes and opens at once; justice arrives thirty years late.

chapters.title: Invitation to the Estate
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV. Wren summons Ansel to the Voss estate at midnight: bring the confession, come alone, or the third victim dies—someone Ansel loves. Beat: cornered resolve; Ansel chooses to walk into the trap rather than let anyone else pay.

chapters.title: The Third Will
chapters.summary: Ansel and Wren, alternating. In Marguerite's preserved bedroom, Wren reveals the third document: Edmund appointed a guardian for his granddaughter—and named the foster sister who once protected Wren in the night: Ansel. Beat: emotional climax of theme; inheritance as obligation, not reward.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV. Rather than fight or flee, Ansel goes live on air from the estate, telling the whole story—Marguerite's murder, Wren's staged killings, her own erased childhood—forcing the truth into daylight where Wren can't be quietly disappeared. Beat: courage as exposure; invisibility surrendered on purpose.

chapters.title: Surrender
chapters.summary: Okafor, POV. Okafor arrives with the confession tape and negotiates Wren's surrender, leveraging the uncle's posthumous guilt and Wren's cooperation to secure manslaughter charges instead of execution-bound murder convictions. Beat: bittersweet mercy; the law bends just enough to hold them all.

chapters.title: Guardian
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV. Months later, Ansel closes the season with the case solved and visits Wren in custody, bringing letters from the foster kids Wren secretly funded for years. Ansel signs the guardianship papers—for Wren's future parole, for the family neither chose but both keep. Beat: resolution; the price of survival becomes the cost of staying.
